target_customer: K-12 teachers (free) and later schools and districts (paid plans per company site); a 501(c)(3) nonprofit
problem: Teachers duplicated lesson-planning work and lacked free, shareable, standards-aligned materials, especially locally relevant content.
business_model: Nonprofit; free library and tools, paid school plan around $5 per user per month and network plans per the company site; early funding from grants and accelerators
product_category: Open educational resources / lesson planning (edtech nonprofit)

founders.name: Varun Arora
founders.background_notes: Per Hechinger Report (2013) he studied One Laptop Per Child and concluded the gap was locally relevant content; one low-quality profile says he was founder and CTO before becoming CEO. An earlier lesson planner was built and shut down within months per the company blog.

competitors.name: Share My Lesson
competitors.what: Free lesson sharing site backed by the teachers union UFT

competitors.name: BetterLesson
competitors.what: Lesson sharing platform created by a Teach for America alum

competitors.name: Teachers Pay Teachers
competitors.what: Marketplace where teachers buy and sell lessons rather than share them free

technical_complexity.rationale: A web library and lesson-plan builder with GitHub-style forking and file import is standard web development; the hard part was curating about 5,000 math documents (three months of curation per TechCrunch).

defensibility.rationale: Content is curated from open teacher blogs and publishers and openly shared; competitors had more funding or union backing, and no lock-in or network effects are documented.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No source shows an incumbent copying or buying OpenCurriculum; no later news found at all after 2014.

market_need_then: The Common Core rollout (2013-2014) created demand for aligned materials; the 2014 launch reported about 6,000 monthly users, and a beta with about 20 teachers claimed 50% saving on first-time planning time (company-sourced).

identity.logo: A plain letter 'O' per a directory listing (low-quality source)
identity.voice_and_tone: Mission-driven; pitched as 'GitHub for educational content' on its own site

branding.community_and_virality: Covered by TechCrunch (2014), Hechinger Report (2013) and K-12 Dive; no evidence of fan community, merch or meme use.

brand_strength.rationale: Descriptive name that says what it is but is easily confused with the broader open-curriculum and OER movement and with other 'Open Curriculum' entities; press coverage was limited to launch moments.

pivots.from: General platform for teachers to create and share materials (launched August 2013)
pivots.to: Curated Common Core math library, later a planning tool with a paid school plan
pivots.why: Founder said broader rivals went too wide; focus on one subject was intentional (TechCrunch 2014)

outcome_analysis: OpenCurriculum launched in August 2013 as a Pittsburgh nonprofit for open lesson sharing, joined YC in the Winter 2014 nonprofit class, and by July 2014 had a 5,000-document math library and about 6,000 monthly users. Its competitors Share My Lesson, BetterLesson and Teachers Pay Teachers were already established and it has no documented grant totals, user growth or exit afterwards; it is still listed as active with a paid school plan, so it survived as a small nonprofit without evidence of scale, and the outcome is best described as stalled or niche rather than failed.
notes: Funding: TechCrunch (2014) names backers Y Combinator, Points of Light Civic Accelerator, ITU, Carnegie Mellon's Institute of Social Innovation and Thrill Mill, with no amounts. An aggregator lists $160K across 2 rounds including a $120K seed in June 2014 and CB Insights lists a Civic Accelerator seed in May 2013; both unverified and not recorded as rounds. Nonprofit, so VC rounds may not apply. YC page says founded 2011; the platform launched August 2013. Status Active agrees with directory; no post-2014 news found in the outcome search (current traction unknown). Paid plan price comes from the company site as read in the earlier depth-1 run and was not re-verified. A CB Insights 'Open Curriculum' entry is likely an unrelated company. Name origin not found. Web Archive skipped. Completeness pass: two seed rounds recorded from aggregators only (Village and The Company Check give $120K in June 2014; CB Insights dates a Civic Accelerator seed to May 2013, and The Company Check says $40K for it while Seedtable says $10K total, so the 2013 amount is null). The CB Insights entry may belong to an unrelated company. Each round rests on a single database; no press states amounts.
